introduction: On this Sunday, Isaiah tells us that God's ways are not our ways, and his thoughts are not our thoughts. In the Gospel, Jesus tells the parable of the landowner who pays the workers hired at the last hour the same as those who worked all day. Paul says, For me, to live is Christ and to die is gain. Let us rejoice in God's generosity.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord is near to all who call on him. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may rejoice in God's generosity to every person, whenever they come. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who come to faith late in life: that they may be welcomed with joy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the unemployed and those who stand idle because no one has hired them: that they may find work and dignity. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are envious of others' blessings: that they may learn to rejoice in God's goodness. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that Christ may be glorified in our bodies, whether by life or by death. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, your ways are higher than our ways and your generosity is beyond measure. Free us from envy, and let us rejoice in your goodness to all. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Is your eye evil because I am good?
reflection.body:
Isaiah invites us to seek God "while he may be found" and promises that he "will freely pardon." Then God explains why his mercy surprises us: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways." God's generosity does not follow our calculations.

In the Gospel, Jesus tells a parable that challenges our sense of fairness. A landowner hires workers at dawn, agreeing to pay them a denarius, a day's wage. He goes out again at nine, at noon, at three, and finally at five o'clock, the eleventh hour, when he finds people standing idle "Because no one has hired us." He sends them all into his vineyard.

In the evening, he pays everyone, beginning with the last, and each receives a denarius. Those who worked all day expect more. When they receive the same, they grumble: "you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat!"

The landowner answers, "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Didn't you agree with me for a denarius?" And he asks, "Isn't it lawful for me to do what I want to with what I own? Or is your eye evil, because I am good?" The problem is not injustice but envy.

The parable speaks about God's grace. Salvation is not a wage earned by hours worked; it is a gift. Those who come to God late in life, even at the last hour, are welcomed with the same love. Those who have served God all their lives are invited not to resent this, but to rejoice in it.

Paul shows what it looks like when Christ is everything: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain."

This week, notice if you feel envy at someone else's blessing, and turn it into thanks. And pray for someone who has not yet come to God: it is never too late.
